title: Folk Art
description: Ten calm essays and portraits on folk art: the quilts of Gee's Bend, Shaker oval boxes, Pennsylvania barn stars, scrimshaw, weathervanes, a self-taught painter, Appalachian baskets, carved decoys, a museum of the overlooked and the alebrijes of Mexico.

lessons.title: The Quilts of Gee's Bend
lessons.summary: In a small Alabama community, women turned worn work clothes into quilts that the art world later recognized as masterpieces.
lessons.text:
In the southwest of Alabama, the Alabama River makes a deep loop, and inside that loop lies a small community called Gee's Bend. Water surrounds it on three sides. Many of the families who live there today are descended from people who were enslaved on the cotton plantation that once covered the land. After slavery ended, the formerly enslaved families stayed, farmed the same fields as tenants, and, through the long winters, made quilts.

They made them because the houses were cold. A quilt began as a pile of what the family could no longer wear: the legs of old work trousers, faded shirts, sacks that had once held flour or feed. Years of hard labor and laundering had softened the cloth, and laundering had faded the blue of the denim to the pale color of a winter sky.

What the women did with these materials is the reason their quilts now hang in museums. A common misconception holds that a good quilt must follow a pattern exactly. The quilters of Gee's Bend ignored that misconception and often worked without such inhibitions. A design might begin as squares inside squares and then wander, the lines growing wider on one side, a strip of red cut short where the cloth ran out. The result is not careless. It is the work of women who knew the rules well enough to bend them, and whose lack of inhibition gave their quilts a strong, living rhythm.

The skill passed from mother to daughter. Girls watched eagerly as the older women cut and sewed, and they eagerly joined in as soon as they could hold a needle. The community was a quiet powerhouse of design, although for most of the twentieth century almost no one outside it knew.

That changed in 2002, when an exhibition of the quilts opened in Houston and later traveled to New York. Critics were amazed. One writer famously compared the quilts with the finest modern art the country had produced, and the comparison, famously bold at the time, no longer seems strange. The radiant oranges and reds of some quilts and the soft, worn blues of others drew crowds who had never thought of a blanket as art. In 2006 the quilts even appeared on a set of postage stamps, small radiant squares on ordinary envelopes.

Two things about the story are especially noteworthy. One is that the makers never set out to impress a museum; they set out to keep their children warm. The other noteworthy point is that the tradition is still alive. Women in Gee's Bend continue to quilt today, and the small community by the river is now recognized as a powerhouse of the nation's art.

Questions:
Why are many families in Gee's Bend connected to the old plantation?
Many of them are descended from people who were enslaved on the cotton plantation that once covered the land.
What materials did the women use for their quilts?
They used old work clothes, faded shirts and sacks, softened by years of labor and laundering.
What common misconception do the Gee's Bend quilts challenge?
They challenge the misconception that a good quilt must follow a pattern exactly.
How was the skill passed on?
Girls watched eagerly as the older women worked, and the skill passed from mother to daughter.
What happened in 2002?
An exhibition of the quilts opened in Houston, and critics were amazed.

lessons.title: The Oval Box
lessons.summary: The Shakers' oval boxes show how a religious community turned careful work into a kind of prayer.
lessons.text:
The Shakers were a religious community that came to New York from England in 1774, led by a woman named Ann Lee. Members renounced marriage and lived together as brothers and sisters. They renounced private property as well and tried to make every task a form of prayer. A saying often linked to Ann Lee sums up the idea: hands to work, hearts to God.

Each village had deacons, men and women chosen to manage its farms, workshops and trade with the outside world. A deacon might oversee the seed business or the making of brooms. The Shakers are often credited with inventing the flat broom, which sweeps far better than a round bundle of straw.

But the object most people picture today is a small oval box. It begins as a thin band of maple. The maker soaks the band in hot water until it can bend without cracking, then wraps it around an oval wooden form. Where the two ends of the band overlap, the outer end has already been cut into several long, pointed fingers.

The fingers are the clever part. Wood swells in damp weather and shrinks in dry weather, and a straight seam would split under the strain. The pointed fingers let the band move a little without breaking. They are held with small copper tacks, driven through and bent over on the inside against an iron rod. Any burr left on a tack is filed away, because a burr would catch on whatever was stored inside. No adhesive is used on the joint. The tacks and the fit do the work, and an adhesive would only stop the wood from moving as it must. Finally, a top and bottom of pine are fitted neatly into the band.

Everything is finished neatly, even inside, where no one will look. Brothers and sisters were taught to be mindful of every step, as if the hidden surfaces mattered as much as the visible ones. Being mindful in this way was not a technique; it was part of their faith.

The Shakers were also known for their music. They had no famous vocalists. The whole community sang together during worship, in songs as plain as their boxes. One of them, written in 1848, is still performed by vocalists and choirs around the world.

Today very few Shakers remain, in a single village in Maine. Yet their name has become a synonym for honest, simple design, and in some shops "Shaker style" is almost a synonym for good taste. Shaker kitchens and chairs are trendy in cities the Shakers never knew. The fashion might have puzzled them, since trendy things come and go, and they built to last a hundred years.

Questions:
What did members of the Shaker community renounce?
They renounced marriage and private property.
What did a deacon do?
A deacon managed farms, workshops or trade, such as the making of brooms.
Why are the ends of the band cut into pointed fingers?
The fingers let the band move a little as the wood swells and shrinks, so it does not split.
Why is no adhesive used on the joint?
The tacks and the fit do the work, and an adhesive would stop the wood from moving.
What has the word "Shaker" become a synonym for?
It has become a synonym for honest, simple design.

lessons.title: Stars on the Barns
lessons.summary: The painted stars on Pennsylvania barns are surrounded by stories, but many historians think they were made mainly for beauty.
lessons.text:
Drive through the farm country of southeastern Pennsylvania in summer, past fields of wheat and barley and pastures where cattle are grazing, and sooner or later you will notice a painted star on the side of a barn. It is usually a circle a few feet across, set high under the roof, with a bright star or flower inside it. Motorists slow down to look, and some stop to take a picture. These designs are often called hex signs, and they belong to the Pennsylvania Dutch.

The name is misleading in two ways. First, the Pennsylvania Dutch are not Dutch. They descend from German-speaking settlers of the eighteenth century, and "Dutch" is an old English version of their own word for German. Second, the word "hex" sounds like the German word for a witch. Many visitors therefore assume that the signs are charms meant to protect the animals and the barley stored in the barn.

Folklore supports this idea to some extent. Pennsylvania German folklore includes healers, blessings and protective sayings, and some farm families did give the stars a quasi-magical meaning. Yet many historians believe that most farmers painted them simply because they liked them. The stars had no ceremonial role. No one blessed them, and no ceremonial words were spoken when they were painted. Their place lies in between: not quite magic, not only decoration, but a quasi-religious habit of beauty passed from parents to children.

Not every Pennsylvania German painted them. The plain churches, such as the Amish and the Mennonites, disapproved of decoration on buildings, and their barns stayed plain. The stars appear mostly on the barns of the so-called church people, Lutherans and Reformed, who did not disapprove of a little color.

The designs themselves feel astronomical: stars with five, six, eight or twelve points, wheels that resemble the sun, petals that seem to turn like a slow galaxy. Some writers have read them as a calendar of the seasons, although there is little evidence for such an astronomical code.

In the twentieth century the signs found a new audience. As more motorists toured the region, writers and travel promoters began to describe the stars as charms, and painters began to sell small round hex signs for porches and kitchens. Each design was given a meaning: a bird for luck, hearts for love, raindrops for good harvests. These generalized meanings were partly invented for visitors, but they have become part of the tradition too. A generalized wish for luck, after all, is something almost anyone can share.

Today fewer barns carry the old stars, because the old barns themselves are disappearing. Where they survive, they remain a pleasant sight for a motorist on a country road: a little sun on a red wall, high above the grazing cattle.

Questions:
Where do the painted stars usually appear?
They appear high on the sides of barns, among fields of barley and pastures where cattle are grazing.
Why is the name "Pennsylvania Dutch" misleading?
The Pennsylvania Dutch are not Dutch; they descend from German-speaking settlers.
Did the stars have a ceremonial role?
No, they had no ceremonial role, and no one blessed them.
Why do Amish barns have no stars?
The Amish disapproved of decoration on buildings.
Where did the generalized meanings of the designs come from?
They were partly invented for visitors, as more motorists toured the region.

lessons.title: Pictures on a Whale's Tooth
lessons.summary: On long whaling voyages, sailors filled empty weeks by carving pictures into whale teeth and bone.
lessons.text:
In the nineteenth century, a whaling voyage from New England could last three or four years. The work came in sudden bursts. When a lookout spotted a whale, the crew lowered small boats and rowed after it, sometimes for hours, until their arms and backs ached with exhaustion. A wounded whale could go on a rampage, smashing a boat with its tail, and the men thrown into the water were often powerless to save themselves. In 1820 a sperm whale on a rampage even sank an entire ship, the Essex. After the chase came more exhaustion, as the crew boiled the whale's fat into oil for days without rest. Then came long, empty weeks of waiting for the next whale, when a ship without wind was powerless to move at all. Life on board was horribly cramped, the food was poor, and the ship smelled horribly of smoke and oil.

To fill those empty weeks, many sailors made scrimshaw. The word means carving or engraving on the teeth and bones of whales, especially the large teeth of the sperm whale. A sailor would first scrape a tooth smooth and polish it, sometimes with the rough skin of a shark. Then, with a knife or a sail needle, he scratched a design into the surface. Finally he rubbed in a dab of black ink and wiped the surface clean, and the fine lines appeared, dark against the pale tooth. A second dab of red or blue might color a flag or a dress.

The pictures are mostly nautical. Ships under full sail, whales rising from the sea, harbors and lighthouses fill the teeth, along with nautical details that sailors knew by heart. Yet many pieces look inward as well as outward. Far from home for years, the men carved portraits of women, houses with gardens, and short verses about the people they loved. A tooth could be a private diary as much as a picture, a way for a lonely sailor to turn his thoughts inward without a word.

The industry that produced scrimshaw reached its pinnacle in the middle of the century, when hundreds of ships sailed from New England ports. The sperm whale was hunted above all for its oil, which lit lamps across the world. It also produced a rare, waxy substance that makers of perfume valued as highly as musk, the strong scent taken from a small deer. Both musk and the whale's wax helped a perfume last longer on the skin.

After the pinnacle came a decline. Petroleum replaced whale oil, and the great fleets disappeared. Today the whales that were hunted are protected by law. Scrimshaw remains as a record of a vanished way of life, dangerous, lonely and patient, written in fine black lines on ivory.

Questions:
Why did the sailors suffer from exhaustion?
They rowed after whales for hours and then boiled the whale's fat into oil for days without rest.
What could a wounded whale do?
It could go on a rampage and smash a boat with its tail.
How did a sailor make the lines of his picture appear?
He rubbed a dab of black ink into the scratches and wiped the surface clean.
Why do many pieces look inward as well as outward?
Far from home, the men carved portraits, houses and verses about the people they loved.
When did the whaling industry reach its pinnacle?
It reached its pinnacle in the middle of the nineteenth century.

lessons.title: The Sculpture on the Roof
lessons.summary: The weathervane, a simple tool for reading the wind, has become a form of sculpture that collectors prize.
lessons.text:
A weathervane has a simple job. It turns on a rod at the top of a building and points into the wind, so that anyone below can tell where the weather is coming from. To do this well, it needs two things. Its tail must be broader than its head, so that the wind pushes the tail away and the head swings around to face the breeze. And its weight must be balanced around the rod, or the gravitational pull on the heavier end will make it lean and stick. Without that balance, gravitational force wins and the wind loses.

For centuries the favorite figure in Europe was the rooster. Roosters stood on ecclesiastical buildings from village chapels to cathedrals. According to a story often repeated, a pope in the ninth century asked every church to display one, to remind believers of the rooster that crowed in the Gospel story of Peter. The rooster became the most familiar ecclesiastical figure and crossed the ocean with the settlers.

In New England, weathervanes came down from the church towers and spread to town halls, stables and farms. A rooster might stand on the roof of a chicken coop, as if guarding the hens in the coop below.

In the nineteenth century, factories began to make them in large numbers. A craftsman hammered thin sheets of copper into iron molds, joined the two halves, and covered the result with gold leaf. A wealthy owner might order a lavish example, with a lavish coat of gold that flashed in the sun. Seen from the street, such a figure seemed to hover in the air with nothing to hold it up, and on a bright day a golden horse would hover above the town like a second sun.

Not every weathervane came from a factory. Farmers cut their own from whatever metal they had: a piece of a fence, an old tin sign, the dented fender of a truck. In the West, a cowboy on a bucking horse, the classic image of the rodeo, became a popular design, and more than one ranch carried a rodeo rider cut from a rusty fender.

Repairing a weathervane on a tall building is still dangerous work. A worker may stand on a narrow ledge high above the street, while the wind it measures pushes against him too. The ledge of a church tower is no place for a careless step.

In the twentieth century, collectors began to see weathervanes as sculpture, and museums brought them indoors to eye level. The prices can stun a newcomer: the finest old examples have sold for more than a million dollars. What would stun the original makers, perhaps, is that their work now stands still in a quiet room, far from the wind it was made to read.

Questions:
Why must a weathervane be balanced around its rod?
Otherwise the gravitational pull on the heavier end will make it lean and stick.
What figure was most common on ecclesiastical buildings in Europe?
The rooster was the most common figure.
Where might a rooster weathervane stand on a farm?
It might stand on the roof of a chicken coop.
What did farmers use to make their own weathervanes?
They used whatever metal they had, even the fender of a truck.
Why is repairing a weathervane dangerous?
A worker may have to stand on a narrow ledge high above the street.

lessons.title: The Painter Who Started with an Errand
lessons.summary: A retired hair stylist teaches herself to paint and finds a bright, personal way of seeing her town.
lessons.text:
For forty-one years, Delia Marsh cut and colored hair in a small shop on the main street of her town. She was, by every account, a good stylist: patient, quick and honest about what a particular haircut could and could not do. When she retired at sixty-eight, she expected to garden, read and help with her grandchildren. She did not expect to become a painter.

It began with an errand. Her granddaughter needed paints for a school project, and Delia bought two sets by mistake. That evening, with the extra set and the back of a cereal box, she painted the view from her kitchen window: a fence, a maple tree and her neighbor's blue truck. "It was terrible," she says, laughing. "But I couldn't stop looking at it."

Six years later, her paintings hang in two galleries and in a regional museum. She has never taken a class. She paints on whatever is at hand, such as plywood, old cupboard doors and cardboard, and she keeps her paint in squeeze bottles that once held ketchup and mustard. A ketchup bottle, she explains, lets her draw a line of color without a brush.

Her subjects are the ordinary sights of the town, made bright and slightly strange: the hardware store under a green sky, the post office in deep snow. Her former customers appear in many of the pictures. "A stylist learns to look at a face for a long time," she says. "I think that's where it started."

She does not measure anything. She eyeballs the size of a building against the trees around it, and she has eyeballed every one of the several hundred paintings she has made. The results are not correct in the way a photograph is correct, but they are often unforgettable. A local critic called her painting of the summer parade unforgettable precisely because the marching band is taller than the church.

There was one long hiatus. Two years after she began, her husband fell ill, and she did not paint for eleven months. When the hiatus ended, the paintings had changed. The skies grew darker, but the windows of the houses were full of warm yellow light.

Visitors often call her a dreamer, and she likes to parry the word with a smile. "I'm not a dreamer," she says. "I paint what's there. I just leave out some of the bad parts." Asked whether that means she avoids sadness, she parries the question again. "There's enough negativity in the world," she says. "Nobody needs me to paint more of it." Her refusal of negativity is a choice, made by someone who has known hard days.

Most mornings she still runs her errands on foot, with a small notebook in her bag.

Questions:
What was Delia's job before she became a painter?
She was a hair stylist for forty-one years.
How did her painting begin?
It began with an errand, when she bought two sets of paints by mistake.
Why does she keep her paint in ketchup bottles?
A ketchup bottle lets her draw a line of color without a brush.
What happened during the hiatus in her work?
Her husband fell ill, and she did not paint for eleven months.
How does she answer when people call her a dreamer?
She parries the word with a smile and says that she paints what is there.

lessons.title: My Grandmother's Egg Basket
lessons.summary: A man remembers how his grandmother in the Kentucky mountains made baskets from white oak and taught him to mend one.
lessons.text:
My grandmother lived at the head of a narrow valley in eastern Kentucky, where the road ended beside a creek. We parked there and walked the last half mile. My father's old truck always announced our arrival. It would backfire once as he turned off the engine, and my grandmother would be waiting on the porch when we arrived. "I heard that truck backfire," she would say, "before I heard you on the path."

She made baskets from white oak, as her mother and grandmother had done. People sometimes speak of such a skill as hereditary, as if it were carried in the blood. It is not hereditary, of course. It is taught, slowly, by one person to another.

The work began in the woods. She chose a young oak with a straight trunk and no knots. Once the tree was cut and split into long sections, she worked them with a knife into thin, flexible strips called splits. Here the first important differentiation was made. Thick, stiff splits became the ribs, the frame of the basket; thin, smooth ones became the weavers that passed over and under the ribs. The differentiation sounds simple, but she said it had taken her years to judge which strip belonged where.

The splits had to stay damp, or they would crack. Water from her roof was diverted through a wooden gutter into an old tub, and the diverted rain kept the splits soft until she needed them.

In the hard years of her youth, her baskets brought in supplemental income, a few cents each. Later, craft schools and shops in the mountains paid fairer prices, and some enlightened teachers and buyers began to treat such baskets as art rather than as cheap containers. Not every buyer was so enlightened, she told me, but the good ones came back. Even so, for her the money was always supplemental. The baskets were made for use, for eggs and beans and lunch in the field.

She also said that an hour of weaving in the evening was good for her sanity. She lived alone after my grandfather died, and in a quiet valley in winter, sanity was not a small thing.

When I was seven, I committed my worst misdemeanor of that summer. I sat on her newest egg basket, finished the night before, and crushed one side flat. My remorse was so great that I hid in the barn. She found me there and said that baskets could be mended and so could boys. She treated my misdemeanor as a lesson. That afternoon she showed me how to cut new ribs and weave them in, and the remorse slowly turned into pride.

I still have that basket. One side is a little uneven, and it is the side I mended.

Questions:
Is basket making a hereditary skill?
No, it is not hereditary; it is taught by one person to another.
What differentiation did the grandmother make between the splits?
Thick, stiff splits became the ribs, and thin, smooth ones became the weavers.
How did she keep the splits damp?
Water from the roof was diverted into an old tub, and the splits soaked there.
What misdemeanor did the boy commit?
He sat on her newest egg basket and crushed one side flat.
How did the grandmother respond to his remorse?
She said that baskets could be mended and showed him how to mend it.

lessons.title: The Ducks in the Scanner
lessons.summary: A museum expert uses a hospital scanner and a paint test to learn the history of three carved decoys.
lessons.text:
On a quiet evening in early spring, a museum expert named Ellen Park carried three wooden ducks into a hospital. The hospital's biomedical imaging center had agreed to let her use its scanner after the last patient had gone home. Machines built to look inside the body work just as well on wood, and biomedical equipment can reveal in a few minutes what would otherwise require taking an object apart.

The ducks were decoys, carved about a century ago. A decoy is a surrogate bird. A hunter floated a group of them on the water so that passing ducks, seeing what looked like a safe flock, would come down to join them. A good surrogate needed only to be convincing from a distance, yet the best makers created birds of real beauty, now collected as folk art.

The first scan showed a hollow body and a strip of lead on the bottom to keep it upright. It also showed, as such scans often do, a group of small bright dots: six round shotgun pellets buried in the wood. A hunter had fired at real ducks and hit the decoy instead. Pellets like these are a sign that a decoy was really used.

The second bird was more puzzling. Its body appeared to be in one piece, but the scan showed a thin dark line where a new head had been attached. The angle of the first image was poor, so the technician had to retake it. He retook it twice before the joint was clear.

A concurrent study of the paint told a similar story. Ellen had also sent tiny samples of paint for an assay, a chemical test that identifies what a material contains. The two concurrent investigations pointed in the same direction. The assay found an original layer containing lead and traces of magnesium, which paint makers once added as a filler. Above it lay an overlay of newer paint containing titanium, a white pigment not common in house paint before the twentieth century. Someone had brushed this overlay on long after the bird was made, perhaps to make it look fresh for a buyer. Without the magnesium in the lower layer, the two layers would have been much harder to tell apart.

The third object was not a duck at all but a fish: a carved cisco, a small silver fish of the northern lakes. Fish decoys like this were lowered through holes in the ice in winter to attract larger fish within reach of a spear. The scan of the cisco showed a lead weight inside its belly.

By midnight Ellen had the images she needed. Each discovery added a line to their history: where they had floated, how they had been mended, and who had tried to make them look younger.

Questions:
Why did Ellen bring the ducks to a biomedical imaging center?
Its scanner can see inside wood without taking an object apart.
What did the first scan show?
It showed a hollow body, a strip of lead and six shotgun pellets buried in the wood.
Why did the technician have to retake an image?
The angle of the first image was poor.
What did the assay find in the paint?
It found an original layer with lead and magnesium and a newer overlay containing titanium.
What was the cisco decoy used for?
It was lowered through the ice to attract larger fish within reach of a spear.

lessons.title: A Museum for the Overlooked
lessons.summary: A small museum in an old bank building collects the art of people who never called themselves artists.
lessons.text:
The building on the corner of Water Street was a bank for most of the last century, and it still looks like one: four stone columns, a heavy front door, and at the foot of each column a scotia, a deep curved molding that holds a band of shadow even at noon. Architects use the scotia to make a column seem to rest lightly on its base. Today the old bank houses a small museum with a long official name, which almost everyone in town shortens to a three-letter acronym. Even the sign on the door uses the acronym.

The museum collects what other museums have overlooked: things made by people who never called themselves artists. Its rooms hold a hooked rug from a farm kitchen and tin toys made by a railroad worker. One case contains small wooden animals carved by a man who had served as a commando during the Second World War. He began carving in a military hospital while he recovered from his wounds, and he continued for the rest of his life. The label explains that the former commando never sold a single animal; he gave them to the children of his town.

Deciding what to accept is the job of the collections subcommittee, whose members meet once a month at a long table in the old bank vault. The subcommittee looks at photographs, hears the story behind each object and then votes. Its main question is simple: does this thing tell us how ordinary people lived and what they found beautiful?

Many objects arrive as gifts. Donors can often deduct the value of a gift from the income on which they pay tax, and the staff explain how to deduct such a gift properly. Last year a retired exec from a software company gave his collection of hand-painted fishing lures. The exec had spent his career protecting banks from malware, and he says that painting lures in his garage was the one place no malware could follow him.

The director admits that the market for folk art is not always kind to a small institution. Prices for some kinds of objects rise and fall sharply, and that volatility makes it hard to plan. A carved figure that sold for a few hundred dollars ten years ago may now sell for thousands, and the volatility works in both directions.

The rules for visitors are short and printed by the door: no food, no flash photography, and no smoking or vaping in the galleries. A guard once had to ask a young man to stop vaping beside a quilt, and he apologized at once. Most visitors walk slowly, and they leave having seen, often for the first time, the art hidden in the objects of an ordinary day.

Questions:
What is a scotia?
A scotia is a deep curved molding at the foot of a column.
Who carved the small wooden animals in one case?
They were carved by a man who had served as a commando during the Second World War.
What does the collections subcommittee do?
It looks at photographs, hears the story behind each object and votes on what to accept.
What did the retired exec give the museum?
He gave his collection of hand-painted fishing lures.
Why is volatility in the market a problem for the museum?
Prices rise and fall sharply, which makes it hard to plan.

lessons.title: Creatures from a Fever Dream
lessons.summary: The brightly painted creatures called alebrijes began in one craftsman's fever dream and grew into a famous folk art.
lessons.text:
In 1936, a craftsman named Pedro Linares fell seriously ill in Mexico City. Linares, who made paper figures for festivals, had a long fever dream during his illness. He saw a strange landscape full of animals that did not exist: a donkey with the wings of a butterfly, a rooster with the horns of a bull, a lion with the head of an eagle. All of them were shouting a single word that meant nothing: "Alebrijes!"

When he recovered, Linares made the creatures. With paper, paste and wire, he built them as he remembered them and painted them in brilliant stripes and spots. He called them alebrijes, after the word in the dream. Linares never set out to be the mastermind of an art movement; he simply made what he had seen. Yet his creatures sold, and over the following decades his work reached collectors and museums. He was later honored as one of his country's great popular artists.

Within a few decades, the idea had reached the state of Oaxaca, in the south, where villagers had long carved small wooden toys and animals. Woodworkers there began to make alebrijes from soft local wood and painted them with the same wild energy. The road to them passes fields of tall plants with sharp leaves, close relatives of the plant from which tequila is made. Here they are made into a different drink, since true tequila comes only from a region farther north. Many family yards are fenced with rows of tall cactus, planted so close together that the cacti form a living green wall.

In the workshops, a single carved jaguar may carry thousands of tiny dots, lines and spirals in a dozen colors. The patterns are so dense that they look almost galactic, and one painter told a visitor that she wanted each creature to carry a galactic sky on its back.

The creatures also borrow from older beliefs. Many regions of Mexico tell of the nahual, a person who can take the form of an animal at night. Outsiders sometimes compare the nahual to the werewolf of old stories in Europe, although in some stories the nahual is a guardian rather than a monster. An alebrije is neither a nahual nor a werewolf, but it shares the old idea that an animal can carry a human spirit.

In recent years alebrijes have traveled far. They are sold in hipster shops in distant cities, and the hipster customers who buy them may know nothing of Linares or his fever. In Mexico City, a yearly parade carries giant alebrijes through the streets. Children watch with open glee and shout out the superpower they imagine for each creature: this one can fly, that one can breathe fire. Flight is the favorite superpower.

The tradition now has no single mastermind; it belongs to thousands of makers. But the glee of those children would surely have pleased the sick man who decided that his dream was worth making real.

Questions:
What did Pedro Linares see in his fever dream?
He saw strange animals that did not exist, all shouting the word "Alebrijes!"
What surrounds many family yards in the carving villages?
Rows of tall cactus form a living wall around them.
Why do the painted patterns look almost galactic?
They are made of thousands of tiny dots, lines and spirals, as dense as a sky full of stars.
What do children do at the parade in Mexico City?
They watch with glee and shout out the superpower they imagine for each creature.
